Three things must stay separate for the team to accept a monorepo without re-litigating ownership: (1) Deploy pipelines – each service keeps its own CI trigger (path-filtered on its directory) and its own production deploy job, so a change to service-A never accidentally bumps service-B's version. This is a CI-configuration boundary, not a repo boundary. (2) Code-review ownership – use CODEOWNERS or a similar mechanism so PRs touching services/b/ require a different reviewer than PRs touching services/c/; this preserves the 'you own your service' mental model and prevents bus-factor collapse. (3) Release cadence – if one service ships weekly and another monthly, each directory gets its own version (via changesets, a per-package version field, or manual tag) so the fast-releasing service does not force the slow one into a release cycle. As long as these three boundaries are codified in the repo (CODEOWNERS file, path-filtered workflow triggers, per-package version fields), the monorepo is operationally equivalent to three repos but with shared tooling. If any of the three cannot be codified – e.g., two services are owned by the same two people and already release together – the monorepo is even lower-risk.

For a four-person team to accept a pnpm monorepo for three Node services, five boundaries must stay independent and one must be accepted as shared. Stay separate: (1) Deploy pipelines—each service deploys on its own trigger, gated by a dependency-graph tool (Turborepo or Nx 'affected' tasks) so a change to service A never rebuilds or redeploys B or C. (2) Ownership—CODEOWNERS maps each service directory to 1-2 specific people so PR review stays small instead of requiring all four. (3) Release cadence—per-package release triggers via Changesets (or semantic-release scoped to a package) so the most-frequent releaser ships without waiting on the others. (4) CI test isolation—each service's test suite runs in its own CI job; a red test in one must not block green deploys of the other two. (5) Feature-flag / environment configuration per service stays in its own env namespace. Must be accepted as shared: a single pnpm-lock.yaml, meaning a major-version bump of a common dependency (e.g. Express→5, Zod→4) propagates to all three services on the next install. The main risk is this lockfile coupling: the team needs a Renovate or Dependabot policy that scopes breaking bumps per package (using pnpm's 'pnpm.overrides' or workspace-protocol ranges) or they will face a 'one bad upgrade blocks three services' incident. Confidence is moderate because these are well-documented pnpm-workspace patterns, but no evidence on the board yet confirms which specific dependencies overlap across the three services.
